Ranked middleweights collide in an important matchup on Saturday night in Las Vegas

        Brendan Allen isn't interested in being anyone's stepping stone. "All In" once again puts his top-five middleweight ranking on the line against someone with more to gain. Allen welcomes rising contender Christian Leroy Duncan to the main event of UFC Fight Night on Saturday at the Meta APEX in Las Vegas.Allen (27-7) can't seem to get ahead, even when he's winning. The longtime middleweight contender is riding a three-fight win streak, but finds himself fighting backward in the rankings again. Allen is understandably frustrated. He'd prefer to fight someone above him, but waiting around won't get him closer to a title shot. That's how he drew Duncan, a dynamic contender who beat Roman Dolidze and Jared Cannonier Those are impressive wins, but Allen warns Duncan against reading too much into them.Sign up for Paramount+ and watch UFC Fight Night for no additional fee -- every UFC numbered event and UFC Fight Night is included with your subscription! Plans start as low as $8.99/month or $89.99/year!"I'm not Roman Dolidze. I'm none of those guys," Allen told CBS Sports. "There's a reason I'm still here: 20 UFC fights against some of the best guys that I could get. His best bet is to catch me with something on Saturday night. Other than that, I'm going to beat him up. I'm going to make it a dogfight. I'm going to get in his face, and I'm going to test him. 
"None of these guys have really tested him like that. Gregory [Rodrigues] did, and look how that turned out. I think I'm a different monster. The best thing I can do is to go out there and be myself."
Duncan (15-2) is finally putting the pieces together. The Englishman has spent more than half his professional MMA career in the UFC, learning on the job against increasingly difficult competition. Consecutive wins over Dolidze and Cannonier have given him the confidence to make a run at the top of the division. He knows Allen's grappling pedigree is legitimate and that he can make fights ugly. But Duncan believes his recent opponents have prepared him for those challenges, even if Allen doesn't."Roman Dolidze: his background and specialty is jiu-jitsu or grappling. Same with Brendan Allen; he's very well versed in that area," Duncan told CBS Sports. "Cannonier is very durable, so that taught me how to deal with a durable fighter that also wants to push the pace and engage.
"I came into the UFC so green, and the fights that I'm getting now, I'm taking a lot from them. Outside of the cage, I'm around some great mentors. The rate at which I'm evolving and learning is now putting me in a position to prepare for the top level and somebody like Brendan Allen."Elsewhere on Saturday's card, Malcolm Wellmaker desperately needs to get back on track. Once considered one of UFC's most promising newcomers, Wellmaker has suffered consecutive losses to Ethyn Ewing and Juan Diaz. A third straight defeat would raise serious questions about his future. All-action veteran Niko Price makes his final walk against Leon Shahbayzan, the younger brother of UFC middleweight Edmen Shahbazyan, on the preliminary card. Another UFC sibling, Ismael Bonfim, also competes on the prelims. His younger brother, Gabriel Bonfim, headlines a Fight Night card next month against Sean Brady.
Let's take a look at the rest of the fight card with the latest odds from DraftKings before getting to a prediction and expert pick on the main event below.UFC Fight Night card, oddsFavoriteUnderdogWeightclassBrendan Allen -125Christian Leroy Duncan +105MiddleweightMatheus Camilo -185Jai Herbert +154LightweightLoopy Godinez -238Ketlen Souza +195Women's strawweightAndre Fili -142Kai Kamaka III +120FeatherweightMalcolm Wellmaker -225Otari Tanzilovi +185BantamweightUFC Fight Night viewing informationDate: Saturday, Oct. 10 | Start time: 8 p.m. ET (Main card), 5 p.m. ET (Prelims)Location: Meta APEX -- Las VegasTV Channel: Paramount+ (subscribe now for as low as $8.99 per month)        PredictionBrendan Allen vs. Christian Leroy Duncan: You have to feel for Allen. He tends to fight to the level of his competition, rising to the occasion and making Reinier de Ridder quit, but struggling more than he should against Chris Curtis and Edmen Shahbazyan. Now he's fighting another dangerous contender down the rankings. Duncan is clearly improving, but his grappling gives me pause. Dolidze and Cannonier took him down eight times combined, with Dolidze enjoying decent control time. Neither veteran is what he once was, and Allen presents a much tougher grappling test.This is Duncan's fight to lose on the feet. Allen absorbs more significant strikes than he lands and isn't much of a knockout threat. Duncan has the tools to put him away early with a highlight-reel finish. However, the longer this fight goes, the more it favors Allen. He's been fighting five-rounders since his regional days. Duncan told CBS Sports that he always trains for 25 minutes, but Saturday could be his first time actually fighting that long. There's a difference. Duncan has never been finished, so I'll lean towards Allen grinding out a decision. A late submission wouldn't shock me either. Pick: Allen via unanimous decision

title: WNBA playoffs: Do the Liberty or Aces have a better chance at coming back? - CBS Sports
description: No team in WNBA history has climbed out of an 0-2 hole in the postseason ... could New York or Las Vegas become t
body:
No team in WNBA history has climbed out of an 0-2 hole in the postseason ... could New York or Las Vegas become the first?
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                            
        
    Oct 9, 2026
                            
                    at
    12:53 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            5 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        History says that the 2026 WNBA Finals are already set; it's just a matter of when the Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream will officially punch their tickets. The Valkyries have taken a 2-0 lead over the reigning champion Las Vegas Aces, while the Dream are up 2-0 on the New York Liberty in their respective semifinal series, both of which will resume Friday. In WNBA history, teams that go up 2-0 in a series are 20-0. That is in part due to a fairly small sample size, but it is more so a reflection of the WNBA's playoff format. Best-of-five series weren't introduced in the WNBA until 2005 and were reserved for the Finals until 2016. Starting in 2016, when the league altered the playoff format to select the top eight teams regardless of conference affiliation, the semifinals were expanded to best-of-five. And as of last season, the Finals are now best-of-seven. So for the first two decades of the league's history, there were only 11 series in which it was even possible for a team to take a 2-0 lead, and up until the 2026 Finals, the only way to pull off a 2-0 comeback was to win three consecutive games in a best-of-five series, presumably against a much better team. 
As such, it makes sense that no team has ever been able to pull off what the Aces and Liberty are about to attempt. As the semifinals shift to Las Vegas and Brooklyn, no one is giving either team much of a chance. But which team has a better chance to make history?Here's what our experts had to say. Who has better chance at coming back from 0-2 deficit?
                    
    
                                            
                    
                                    Lindsay Gibbs
                            
            
                    
    
                                            
                    
                                    Jack Maloney
                            
            
                            
    
                                                
                    
    
        
                            Aces
                    
    
    
                            
    
                                                
                    
    
        
                            Liberty
                    
    
    Gibbs: Let's caveat this: I picked the Liberty and Aces to win these series, and didn't think either team would go winless in the first two games, even though they started on the road. But both the Dream and Valkyries have played inspired basketball so far and have been the better teams, bar none. Recency bias is real, and right now, it's hard to see either of these teams advancing to the WNBA Finals.But, if any team is going to make WNBA history, it is going to be one of these squads -- championship cores with the two best players in the world, Breanna Stewart and A'ja Wilson, leading the way. I'm completely split on which one has the best shot, though.The Liberty are, in my opinion, simply a better team than the Aces. They have more depth, length and versatility, and just a few days ago against the Minnesota Lynx, they looked unstoppable as they knocked out the No. 1 seed. The physicality of the Dream has clearly rocked them -- they had 19 turnovers in Game 1 and 16 in Game 2. That is possible to clean up. If Stewart keeps doing Stewie things, Jonquel Jones and Leonie Fiebich rediscover their first-round form and Sabrina Ionescu recreates magic in Barclays, which she's been wont to do in the playoffs, it is easy to see how New York could turn this around -- especially if Jordin Canada and DeWanna Bonner come back to earth a bit offensively. But right now, the Liberty look gassed; it is hard to trust Liberty coach Chris DeMarco to push the right buttons and, to use an official playoff stat, the Dream are absolutely crushing the Liberty in terms of vibes and cohesiveness, having won nine games in a row and 13 of their last 14.

        
            
                WNBA semis winners and losers: Angel Reese proves clutch as Liberty, Aces face elimination after Game 2 losses
                
                    Jack Maloney                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
While I'm worried about DeMarco, I'm also worried that Aces coach Becky Hammon is simply out of buttons to push in Vegas. They were thin coming into the postseason with NaLyssa Smith out and Dana Evans and Stephanie Talbot both in questionable health, and now Jewell Loyd injured her leg in Game 1, was out for Game 2 and is questionable for Game 3. While Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase truly trusts 10 players on her roster, Hammon struggles to get to five. The only reason I believe the Aces can turn things around is that they have Wilson, who just won her fifth MVP. And honestly? That's a pretty great reason. If Loyd returns and Jackie Young can get closer to the 48.8% she shot from the field during the regular season, rather than the 27.7% she's averaging this series, the Aces can beat the Valkyries three times in a row. After all, Vegas swept the regular-season series.Maloney: Let's start with Aces-Valkyries. There's no reason to trust the Valkyries' offense, which routinely goes ice cold for long stretches. They're shooting 39.4% for the series, and that could always get worse. But we know their defense will show up, and the Aces haven't found any consistent answers there. Jackie Young has been shut down (25 points on 22 shots), A'ja Wilson hasn't been able to dominate and they're shooting 38.7% as a team. So far, their Aces' best offense has been getting to the free-throw line, where they're 34 of 41 (82.9%) in the series.
Suddenly flipping that trend against one of the best defenses in WNBA history would be a monumental task in the best of circumstances. The Aces will have to do so with an injured or banged-up supporting cast. NaLyssa Smith is out for the season, Dana Evans suited up in Game 2 for the first time since Sept. 22 and both Stephanie Talbot and Jewell Loyd are questionable for Game 3 with leg injuries. At a certain point, Wilson, Young and Chelsea Gray can only do so much.And so, I think the answer has to be the Liberty, who have either won or tied six of the nine quarters (including overtime) in the first two games against the Dream, and are having no trouble scoring when they can actually get a shot up at the rim. The Liberty are shooting 48.8% from the field, including 43.4% from 3-point range.The Dream have taken a 2-0 lead in this series by dominating the margins. They've forced 38 turnovers, which they've turned into a staggering 60 points, have grabbed 20 offensive rebounds, which they've turned into 25 second-chance points and have a 29-8 edge in fastbreak points. Cutting down on turnovers against Atlanta's elite defense and controlling the boards against Angel Reese is much easier said than done, but you can see a path to a comeback for the Liberty if they can clean those things up, especially with Allisha Gray still questionable for Game 3 due to a hand injury.

title: 2026 NFL trade deadline: Loss won't sway Jerry Jones from improving Cowboys, which players will they target? - CBS Sports
description: Despite a stunning home loss to Tampa Bay, Dallas sits at 2-3 in a wide-open NFC East with enough draft capital t
body:
Despite a stunning home loss to Tampa Bay, Dallas sits at 2-3 in a wide-open NFC East with enough draft capital to make another splash before the deadline
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 9, 2026
                            
                    at
    12:40 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            7 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        ARLINGTON, Texas -- The Dallas Cowboys (2-3) couldn't have done much more to embarrass themselves than what they did in their 24-16 head-scratcher of a loss against the previously-winless Tampa Bay Buccaneers (1-4) on "Thursday Night Football" to kick off Week 5. The Cowboys trudged off their home field at AT&T Stadium on Thursday while being serenaded by a chorus of boos, and they earned every bit of it. Tampa Bay entered the game with undrafted rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels making his second career start in place of an injured Baker Mayfield, and when the clock hit zero, he was walking off the field with the third-largest upset win, as a 9.5-point underdog, by an undrafted rookie quarterback since the 1970 AFL/NFL merger, per CBS Sports Research. Daniels was an efficient 19 for 25 passing with 189 yards and a touchdown while rushing for 23 yards on 7 carries. Even more damning was allowing Buccaneers running back Bucky Irvin to explode for a career-high 165 yards rushing and a touchdown on 21 carries for a 7.9 yards per carry average. Entering Thursday, he had averaged just 59.2 rushing yards per game across the last two seasons.   Dallas' loss was so disheartening that someone yelled "embarrassing" at Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott as he walked through the bowels of the stadium to the locker room by himself after the game.   "It's a loss we're supposed to have, definitely supposed to have. To use the word embarrassing — it's tough," Prescott said. "I feel like I'm discrediting the NFL if I use that [the word embarrassing] and particularly the Tampa Bay Bucs, the great Todd Bowles. … [But] when a winless team comes into your home stadium on a Thursday night primetime game, yeah, we're supposed to win that."
Was the loss embarrassing enough to dissuade Cowboys owner and general manager Jerry Jones from no longer pursuing additional win-now trades? He already traded a 2027 sixth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick to the Pittsburgh Steelers for 26-year-old cornerback Joey Porter Jr. Porter Jr. didn't make his home debut Thursday night because of "flu-like" symptoms. Jones' answer to that question is simple: Nope, I'm still open for business. The man is set to turn 84 years old on Oct. 13, so he's open to doing what he can to win a fourth Super Bowl right now. "The future capital, I wouldn't give it up for a player who didn't have some future or the potential of future that you could add years to. The future capital that you have are draft picks. Those guys have question marks with them too. So if we do see an opportunity, and it fits for us, we'll take a good look at it," Jones said postgame. "This isn't fold the tents here. We are 2-3, didn't expect to be 2-3. Didn't expect this Tampa team to come here 0-4 either. They got a lot of good players. Unquestionably, they were the better team tonight."  Jones does say a lot of eyebrow-raising things, but it is fair for him to envision the NFC East division to still be up for grabs for his Cowboys, as surreal as that sentiment feels in this moment. The New York Giants are 3-1, but their ceiling is limited by the season-ending knee injury to quarterback Jaxson Dart. Fill-in Jameis Winston ranks dead last in the NFL in completion percentage at 55.1% this season. The Giants are also without three-time Pro Bowl edge rusher Brian Burns, their best pass rusher, whose 16.5 sacks ranked second in the league in 2025, for the rest of the year after he tore his ACL and meniscus. The Philadelphia Eagles (2-2) are fresh off an epic meltdown home loss of their own against the Los Angeles Rams in which they blew a double-digit lead and went 0-12 in third-down conversion attempts. 
In the aftermath of that loss, Eagles six-time Pro Bowl right tackle Lane Johnson retired on Tuesday, and Philadelphia then traded two-time Pro Bowl offensive lineman Cam Jurgens to the Baltimore Ravens. That's on top of their CVS receipt-length injury list. The Washington Commanders are 1-3, and quarterback Jayden Daniels is once again dealing with an elbow injury. As a refresher before we dive into the trade candidates, here is a look at the draft picks the Cowboys still own the rights to in the event Jones wants to continue doubling down on the 2026 season.Dallas draft picks available 2027 first-round pick (the lesser of their own and the Green Bay Packers')2027 second-round pick2027 fourth-round pick (via Pittsburgh Steelers)2027 seventh-round pick (San Francisco 49ers' pick from a trade with the Houston Texans)2028 first-round pick2028 third-round pick2028 fourth-round pick2028 fifth-round pick2028 sixth-round pick2028 sixth-round pick (via New Orleans Saints)All seven of their 2029 draft picks Here is a look at three players Jones could trade for and "add years to" to win now and over the next season or two. 
Trade candidates
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Chargers EDGE Tuli TuipulotuThis is the big fish right here. The Cowboys currently rank eighth-worst in the NFL in quarterback pressure rate (32.7%) and fifth-worst in sack rate (3.4%). Their pass rush is one of their most glaring remaining needs on defense. Two of their veteran, Pro Bowl edge rushers they acquired this offseason, Rashan Gary and Von Miller, look to be past their expiration date, and the Cowboys have yet to be able to replace All-Pro Micah Parsons' production after trading him to the Green Bay Packers just before the start of the 2025 season.Should Jones be comfortable parting with high-round draft capital, Los Angeles Chargers 24-year-old Pro Bowl edge rusher Tuli Tuipulotu makes a lot of sense. The age is right, and like Porter Jr., he is a former second-round pick in the final year of his rookie deal, looking to cash in on a large, new deal. Tulipulotu's contract situation could make him available in a trade should the 0-4 Chargers decide to have a fire sale ahead of a highly anticipated 2027 NFL Draft class. He erupted for 13.0 sacks, the sixth most in the NFL, and 70 quarterback pressures, the 11th most in the league, in 2025 en route to earning his first Pro Bowl selection in 2025, and he's on pace for another strong season through the first quarter of 2026. He's up to 2.0 and 14 quarterback pressures already this season, despite Los Angeles having spent the sixth-most time in the NFL trailing their opponents at 2:13:59. 
This is the splash move if Jerry truly wants to be "all in" again. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Dolphins LB Jordyn BooksThe Dallas Cowboys reportedly tried to trade for Miami Dolphins linebacker Jordyn Brooks in the offseason, when he had just one year left on his contract, before Miami extended Brooks on a three-year, $48 million contract with $35 million guaranteed in the summer. However, the Dolphins are in the middle of a tear-it-down-to-the-studs rebuild in Year 1, with new head coach Jeff Hafley and new general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan, both of whom come from the Green Bay Packers' draft-and-develop franchise model. Miami is 0-4 and has the NFL's worst scoring offense (11.5 points per game), and is the only team that has not led at any point in 2026. The Dolphins are also paying more for players not on their roster (an NFL-record $179 million in dead cap hits) than the players on their roster ($156 million).   Brooks is 29 years old and under contract through the 2029 season, his age-32 season. That's basically the rest of his prime. Jones not having to worry about Brooks' contract situation is likely a relief, and on a hopeless 2026 Dolphins team, he is still a bright spot. Pro Football Focus grades Brooks as the NFL's No. 12 overall linebacker with a defensive grade of 82.7. He would also be an immediate help to the Cowboys' league-worst run defense, which is allowing an average of 168.4 yards per game. Brooks ranks as PFF's No. 4 linebacker against the run with an 82.7 run defense grade. 

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Broncos WR/Returner Marvin Mims Jr. One might look at this trade candidate and think, "Wait, a minute. Dallas is loaded at wide receiver with CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens!" Yes, that is true, but this trade is more about special teams with a little bit of potential WR3 or WR4 upside. Denver Broncos wide receiver Marvin Mims Jr. is still a developing wide receiver at 24 years old, but he is already one of the NFL's best return men. Mims Jr. is a two-time Pro Bowl returner and earned first-team All-Pro returner accolades in 2024 when he led the NFL with a 15.7 yards per punt return average. He has both a kick and a punt return touchdown in his career, and he led the NFL with 452 punt return yards in 2025. Dallas does have a three-time Pro Bowl and 2024 first-team All-Pro return man in KaVontae Turpin, but the shine may be wearing off the TCU product. He had a brutal fumble on a kickoff return in the loss to the Buccaneers on Thursday, and the 5-foot-7-inch, 170-pound return man is now 30 years old. 
Turpin still remains one of the shiftiest and speediest returners in the league, but at his age and size, Dallas might want someone younger and slightly bigger in Mims, who is 5-feet-11-inches tall and weighs 182 pounds. The Cowboys might be able to get a draft pick for shipping Turpin out, and they could perhaps use that and another later-round pick to bring in a younger, bigger replacement. Plus, Mims went to high school down the street from the Cowboys' team facility, The Star, at Lone Star High School. Jones loves his hometown and Texas ties.

Here's what to watch as college football's elite teams begin to separate themselves

        We're approaching the midway point of the college football season, and we're really getting into the meat of conference play. The cream is starting to rise, and there will be more separation this weekend.That will be the case on Saturday afternoon when No. 21 UCLA visits No. 13 Oregon. The Bruins are 4-0, but their strength of schedule leaves a lot to be desired. The Ducks, on the other hand, have looked mortal through one month. Either UCLA will assert itself as a premier Big Ten team or Oregon will take another step toward reaching its championship potential.There will be a showdown between two of the best teams in the SEC as No. 6 Alabama hosts No. 2 Georgia. Both programs have been demolishing opponents, and that should make for a heavyweight fight within the confines of Bryant-Denny Stadium.
        
            
                Week 6 College Football Playoff impact games: Georgia, Alabama meet with potential No. 1 ranking on the line
                
                    Shehan Jeyarajah                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
Elsewhere, Indiana travels to Nebraska in a battle of unbeaten teams with underwhelming resumes. Then, in Dallas, the Red River Rivalry writes another chapter in what figures to be a four-quarter defensive struggle.To help you prioritize which games to watch, we've built a handy viewer's guide.
The best gamesNo. 7 Indiana at Nebraska -- 12 p.m. on Fox, Fubo (try for free): Neither of these teams has built a particularly impressive resume, but someone's is about to get a lot stronger. Indiana has handled its business as the defending champions -- even if it hasn't always been pretty -- but this is the first time the Hoosiers haven entered a truly hostile environment. Meanwhile, "Lanterns" star Matt Rhule is still looking for his first top-25 win with the Huskers. Anthony Colandrea has reinvigorated the offense, but the defense will get a big challenge as it tries to withstand the Indiana offense.No. 1 Texas vs. Oklahoma -- 3:30 p.m. on ABC, Fubo (try for free): "Throw out the records" is a rivalry game cliche, but this is one of the rare occasions when it actually applies. That's good news for the Sooners, who have a much worse record entering this game. Oklahoma is searching for answers on offense, and had a bye week to find some. If the Sooners don't have another gear on that side of the ball, they'll get eaten alive by the Texas defense. Either way, the Oklahoma defense will probably have to shoulder the burden as it faces a Longhorns offense that hasn't exactly been firing on all cylinders either.
        
            
                Oregon QB Dante Moore ruled out vs. UCLA as Dylan Raiola nears first Ducks start
                
                    Austin Nivison                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
No. 21 UCLA at No. 13 Oregon -- 3:30 p.m. on CBS, CBSSports.com, Paramount+: The Bob Chesney era is off to a great start at UCLA, but the Bruins will get their biggest test of the season when they travel to Oregon. UCLA runs the ball as well as any team in the country, but that ability will certainly be tested against the Ducks' front seven. Meanwhile, Oregon has yet to look like a bona fide national championship contender, and it's already suffered one major upset. Can the team get rolling with Dylan Raiola making his first start for the Ducks in place of the injured Dante Moore?No. 2 Georgia at No. 6 Alabama -- 7:30 p.m. on ABC, Fubo (try for free): Rain, shine or tropical storm, there will be a football game between two of the top three teams in the SEC this weekend. The battle between Keelon Russell and the Bulldogs defense will be tremendous television. Russell and the Crimson Tide have hung big numbers on the scoreboard, and Georgia has yet to surrender more than 20 points in a single game. For the Bulldogs, Gunner Stockton looks like an improved quarterback, but we'll find out just how real that is in Tuscaloosa.
No. 23 Boise State at Fresno State -- 10:30 p.m. on CW, Fubo (try for free): Welcome to the new Pac-12 After Dark. Boise State is very much in the running for a College Football Playoff berth, but don't count out Fresno State, which is hoping to build its resume with a win over the Broncos this weekend. Since its season-opening loss to Oregon, Boise State has been rolling. The Broncos have won each of their last four games by at least 14 points, but that streak will be tough to extend against the Bulldogs.         Just five teams remain in the 2026 MLB playoff field. The Dodgers, Rays and Brewers all advanced to the LCS round on Wednesday night, knocking the Braves, Yankees and Padres out, respectively. The two-time reigning champion Dodgers will face the Brewers in the NLCS for the second straight year, while the Rays await the Guardians-White Sox winner in the ALCS. Guardians vs. White Sox is the only LDS series still going, and Cleveland kept its season alive with a 9-5 road win in Game 4. title: Mike Ditka, Hall of Fame tight end and Bears Super Bowl-winning coach, dies at age 86 - CBS Sports
description: Ditka was a fixture in the NFL for more than 50 years
body:
Ditka was a fixture in the NFL for more than 50 years
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 9, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:48 am ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Mike Ditka, a Hall of Fame tight end and the coach of the Chicago Bears' only Super Bowl championship team, has died at the age of 86, his family announced on Friday. Ditka's long list of accomplishments includes being a member of both the College and Pro Football Hall of Fame, the 1961 NFL Offensive Player of the Year and a two-time NFL Coach of the Year. The first tight end inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame, Ditka's No. 89 has been retired by the Bears. "It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and friend, Mike Ditka," his family said in a statement. "While the world knew Mike as a Hall of Fame football player, legendary coach, and leader of the Chicago Bears' Super Bowl XX championship team, we knew him as the heart of our family."Mike will be missed beyond measure and remembered forever."Ditka was raised in Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, the same area that produced fellow Hall of Famers Tony Dorsett, Ty Law and Darrelle Revis. He went to the University of Pittsburgh, aspiring to be a dentist. It quickly became clear, however, that football would become Ditka's chosen profession. 
Following a decorated college career (he averaged a whopping 24.3 yards per catch at Pitt), Ditka was taken with the fifth overall pick in the 1961 NFL Draft. That season, he became the first tight end in NFL history to go over 1,000 yards receiving. Ditka led the Bears to the 1963 NFL title and later helped the Cowboys capture their first title at the end of the 1971 season. He caught a touchdown pass from Roger Staubach during Dallas' 24-3 win over Miami in Super Bowl VI. 
After retiring as a player, Ditka joined Tom Landry's staff as the Cowboys' special teams and receivers coach. He won a second Super Bowl in that role at the end of the 1977 season. 
In 1982, Ditka returned to Chicago to become the Bears' coach. Just three years after landing the job, Ditka helped lead the Bears to an 18-1 record that concluded with a 46-10 win over the Patriots in Super Bowl XX. In Chicago, Ditka enjoyed a successful (albeit at times volatile) working relationship with legendary defensive coordinator Buddy Ryan, who was the architect of the Bears' vaunted 46 defense. Fittingly, both men were carried off the field following Chicago's victory over New England. "The '85 beers would not have been the '85 beers without Buddy Bryan," Ditka said in 2018 shortly after Ryan's passing. "We won the Super Bowl because of our defense. I mean, you'd have to be a fool to say otherwise. We had great players on offense, and Walter Payton and Willie Gault and some of the other guys we had, and we had a wonderful offensive line. But our defense is why we won." 
Ditka's success as the Bears' coach made him an icon in the Windy City. He was imitated often on Saturday Night Live, where he was affectionately referred to as "Da Coach." Bears fans embraced his tough, rugged demeanor that fit Chicago's blue-collar spirit like a glove.  
Ditka coached the Bears for 11 years before getting into broadcasting in 1993. He briefly returned to the sidelines with the Saints in 1997. His tenure in New Orleans is largely remembered for trading each of the team's 1999 NFL Draft picks to Washington in exchange for the No. 1 overall pick. The Saints used that pick to draft Ricky Williams, the reigning Heisman Trophy Winner. Ditka returned to broadcasting following his run in New Orleans (and in 2005, starred alongside Will Ferrell in the movie "Kicking and Screaming") but had kept a low profile in recent years. In 2020, he was at the Super Bowl as part of the NFL's 100th Anniversary All-Time Team.

title: Are the Texans cooked after their 0-4 start? Why a sliver of hope still remains for Houston - CBS Sports
description: The Texans are winless and on the brink of losing their season, but there are at least a few reasons to wait it o
body:
The Texans are winless and on the brink of losing their season, but there are at least a few reasons to wait it out a little longer
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 9, 2026
                            
                    at
    12:28 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Going into the 2026 season, the Houston Texans were a trendy dark horse pick to come out of the AFC and make the Super Bowl. On the backs of one of the best defenses in the NFL and a retooled offensive line in front of QB CJ Stroud, the Texans were expected to wreck shop through the AFC.Four games into the season, and we still haven't seen the Texans pick up their first win. The offense has been inconsistent, battling through Nico Collins injuries and an offensive line that hasn't truly gelled together yet. Defensively, a unit that was supposed to be elite has looked the opposite during the early quarter of the season. Their 2.42 points allowed per drive is the highest through four games since Demeco Ryans took over as head coach and is a far cry from last season's 1.21 points allowed per drive. The spin zone for Texans fans is that this organization came back from being 0-3 to making the playoffs in 2025, but 0-4 feels like a deep hole to climb out of, with the 1992 Chargers as the only team to make the playoffs after starting 0-4. The Texans go into their game against Tennessee (who is also winless) desperately needing a win to keep their season alive, but how and why did we get to this point?
Houston, we have a problem: How the Texans got hereLet's start with the bad for the Texans right now, which focuses on the defensive side of the ball. Yes, they've faced a lot of the NFL's best offenses in Buffalo, Cincinnati and Dallas to start the season, but something about the group has felt…off. It's why head coach Demeco Ryans took back playcalling duties from defensive coordinator Matt Burke and why the team overall has looked the way it has. For the 2026 Texans to work, this defense would have to be an elite group as the offense found its way and gelled together, and the defense hasn't been that. Again, they've faced some tough offenses and were without starting LB Azeez Al-Shaair in their loss to the Cowboys, but the underlying metrics this season have revealed a much larger problem.Through four games, the Texans are allowing the most explosive passes since Demeco Ryans took over. Despite still being a top ten defense based on success rate (how often teams move the ball against them), they're 25th in defensive EPA per play (geared more toward explosiveness) and 28th in explosive play rate allowed this season. They've given up far too many big passes, and it's taken a major hit to their entire defense. 
Now, the first issue seems to be communication, which is why Ryans is taking over. There have been far too many coverage busts in the secondary for a unit as talented as the Texans. This play against the Cowboys is a good example. The Cowboys are running a deep crosser for WR Ceedee Lamb, with WR George Pickens running a clear-out route. The Texans are running Cover 3, but CB Derek Stingley Jr is trying to pass off the crossing route of Lamb to S Calen Bullock, because he has a better angle on it. Bullock, however, sticks with Pickens' deep clear-out route, and Lamb runs wide open.
On the play that would set up the eventual game-winning touchdown for the Cowboys, CB Kamari Lassiter bites on a sluggo from Pickens, and S Reed Blankenship gets too sucked into the middle of the field. That leaves a void for QB Dak Prescott to find Pickens for a big play. Lassiter and Blankenship (both good players) have had rough starts to the season. Lassiter has especially been picked on in the passing game, giving up a 110.4 passer rating when in coverage.
Does hope remain for the Texans?While it hasn't been great for the secondary, I definitely think that's fixable. What might not be fixable is their run game, which looks awful once again. After investing a lot in the offseason in revamping the offensive line and running back room, the Texans' run game is…worse than it was last year through four games. 
The unit is averaging -0.15 EPA/rush, a 32.9% rushing success rate (excluding scrambles) and a paltry 3.5 yards per carry. The entire goal of this offense was for the run game to help grind teams down so Stroud doesn't have to carry the entire offense, and so far, the Texans' run game hasn't held up its part of the bargain. The idea of condensing formations and being a ground-and-pound team is great in theory, but the Texans find themselves running into a wall — literally — and asking CJ Stroud to save them from themselves.Now, if there's a silver lining to the season so far, it's been that Stroud has been HOOPIN to start the season. Stroud is 11th in EPA per dropback and 13th in dropback success rate, looking more like the player we saw in 2023 than the guy we saw in 2024 and 2025. His pocket movement has improved significantly, and his elite ball placement has remained. This touchdown to Nico Collins was just exquisite QB play.
Do I think the Texans are cooked for this season? I'm choosing to hold on a little bit longer. All of their losses have been one-score losses, and the QB is playing at a high level right now. Once the secondary resolves its communication issues, the defense should pick up again. A 0-4 start is a steep hill to climb out of, but I think the Texans can get out of it.

title: Anxiety Rankings, Week 6: Brent Venables under pressure, USC and Penn State both need wins - CBS Sports
description: There are very few things in life that can stir emotions within you like college football. For four months a year, millions of Americans
body:
There are very few things in life that can stir emotions within you like college football. For four months a year, millions of Americans decide to put their mental well-being in the hands of a collection of 18- to 24-year-old men they do not know personally. All they know is that they've chosen to wear their preferred uniform. Sometimes this decision brings joy. Other times it brings pain.But what it always brings as kickoff draws near every week is anxiety. There's always the nervous energy of the unknown heading into a game. You can never be sure how things will go, and where the rollercoaster will take you. However, while we all feel it, some of us feel it more than others, and each week, The Anxiety Rankings aim to find the five most anxious places in the country.Welcome to Week 6. Try to stay calm. You'll fail, but try all the same.1. Brent VenablesI don't know whether he did it intentionally or not, but there was a moment when Brent Venables was asked during a press conference this week what a win over Texas would mean. He took a breath and then said under his breath, but loud enough for the microphone to pick it up, "it would turn around our season."He then went into his normal voice and gave a standard coaching answer about not being where they want to be as a football team, needing to play our best football, focusing on an opportunity to compete, and so on and so forth as is prescribed in the press conference manual handed out to all college football coaches before each season. But everything he needed to tell you was in that first sentence that he may not have meant for you to hear.
A win this week against Texas would turn around Oklahoma's season, and not simply in the typical fashion of beating your most-hated rival. A win would get the Sooners to 3-2 on the year and 1-1 in the SEC. It would help heal the wounds of an embarrassing 41-13 blowout loss to Georgia two weeks ago. A win would bring confidence to the locker room and tell the country that, while the Sooners got off to a slow start, they're still a team capable of beating the No. 1 team in the country. They're still a team that has an opportunity to compete for the SEC and the College Football Playoff.But a loss? Hoo boy. A loss could send the season spiraling past the point of return. It would drop the Sooners to 2-3 on the season and 0-2 in the SEC. Any chance of even pretending this team can get back to the playoffs would be quickly dismissed. After all, there are still four more games on the schedule against teams that are currently ranked, even if none of them are the caliber of Georgia or Texas.It would also be Oklahoma's third-straight loss to the hated Longhorns, and fourth loss in the last five years since Venables took over. Oklahoma hasn't lost three straight to Texas since the stretch between 1997 and 1999. Those first two losses belong to John Blake, who was not given the chance to lose a third. The last one belonged to Bob Stoops, who wouldn't suffer another loss to the Longhorns for another six years.
Venables was given a contract extension following last year's playoff appearance, so there's no guarantee Oklahoma would look to move on. However, this is college football. If you lose to your rival for the fourth time in five years and it leads to the season collapsing, well, we've seen schools pay a lot of money to erase mistakes before, haven't we?I'd be mumbling to myself too if I were in Venables' shoes.2. Week 6 Anxiety Bowl - USC at Penn StateIt's White Out week at Penn State, and I'm not sure if anybody is excited about it. Penn State enters the game having lost two straight. All the excitement of a new coaching staff and a 3-0 start to the season went out the window quickly following two ugly losses to Wisconsin and Northwestern. Against Wisconsin, the offense was horrific, but at least the defense held its own.Last week against Northwestern, the Nittany Lions had nothing. They scored only 13 points, and the defense let the Wildcats run wild for 413 yards. Seriously, there isn't a typo there. It's supposed to say 413. Northwestern averaged 7.5 yards per carry on 55 attempts. It looked like a high school powerhouse playing some small 7-man team from the boonies out there. And now the team returns home to play the team that was supposed to be one of the two toughest on its schedule this year.
If Penn State loses, they'll be 3-3 on the season, and Matt Campbell will become the first Penn State coach to start his tenure 3-3 since Joe Paterno in 1966. With a road trip to Michigan looming, a 3-4 start becomes a very real possibility, as does the idea of missing a bowl game. If that happens, it'll be the first time Penn State missed a bowl (outside the COVID season of 2020) since 2013, right before Bill O'Brien was replaced by James Franklin.But will Penn State lose to USC? That's what makes this The Anxiety Bowl, because would you believe me if I told you that USC is the underdog? That's right, the 5-1 Trojans, whose only loss is to Oregon, are underdogs to a Penn State team that's lost two straight and just got run over like a squirrel crossing the street in heavy traffic. And it makes sense!This is USC on the road under Lincoln Riley. The results haven't been great! The Trojans are 11-10 on the road under Riley, and only 4-7 since joining the Big Ten. When having to leave the West Coast for Big Ten games, they've lost to Maryland, Minnesota and Illinois. Earlier this season, they won at Rutgers, but by a score of 42-35. Rutgers is in far worse shape than Penn State.
So if you're USC and you lose this game, your Big Ten and playoff hopes are essentially done. It's hard to imagine 7-2 gets you to the Big Ten Championship Game, though it's certainly not impossible. What is nearly impossible, though, is finishing 7-2 in the Big Ten. Not when you have games left against Ohio State and Indiana. It's not Happy Valley this weekend. It's Anxiety Alley.3. Nebraska fansNebraska fans have plenty of battle scars to help them deal with the anxiety that comes with rooting for the Cornhuskers, but one of the problems with being punched in the stomach so many times is you have a distinct idea of how it feels, and you don't want to feel it again.So, sure, the Huskers are off to a 5-0 start. The offense doesn't seem to miss Dylan Raiola very much, as Anthony Colandrea's been a good fit in Dana Holgorsen's scheme. Sometimes divorce is the best thing for both parties, and so far that feels like the case in Lincoln.
But Nebraska fans have seen this movie before, too. The team got off to a 5-1 start last year with a close loss to Michigan before finishing the regular season 7-5. In 2024, a 5-1 start ended at 6-6. So you can understand why some Nebraska fans might be hesitant to get overly excited by a 5-0 start this year, particularly when you've played one of the easiest schedules in the country (it generally falls between 120th and 130th depending on your favored metric). It's about to get much more difficult this week. The defending champions are coming to town, and Curt Cignetti's Indiana team isn't known for taking it easy on opponents when it gets the chance. If you're a Nebraska fan, you probably want to be excited about the opportunity to announce to the world that things have changed, but you can't escape that voice in the back of your head whispering, "here comes the doooooooooooooom."The good news for Nebraska is that this isn't a must-win situation. Your season isn't on the line. Frankly, hanging around and keeping it close would probably be a good sign about the team moving forward, even if you don't pull off the upset. 
The bad news is it won't get any easier. Next week you're on the road for Oregon, and you still have dates with Ohio State and Iowa to contend with. But a close loss against Indiana at least gives you the confidence to believe you can flirt with playoff contention for the rest of the season, and maybe shock the world with an upset. But a blowout loss would erase all the fun of that 5-0 start very quickly and make you wonder if you're in for another late-season collapse.4. VirginiaLast week was not supposed to happen. It's one thing to lose to Florida State on the road, even this 2026 version of Florida State. It's not ideal, but it's understandable. What isn't as understandable is getting trounced by these Seminoles. The Florida State offense looked terrific in a 38-7 win over the Cavaliers, and suddenly a Virginia season that looked promising is on the verge of being lost.The Hoos were a big surprise last year, reaching the ACC Championship. They got off to another excellent start this season with a season-opening 34-8 win over NC State. Sure, they lost to West Virginia, but it wasn't a conference loss, so you could survive it. But now you're 3-2 on the season, and as you look back at the schedule you've played, things no longer seem all that impressive.
NC State is 3-2. The Florida State team that killed you is 3-2. The West Virginia team that beat you has lost two straight since, and is 3-2 as well. Your other wins have been against Norfolk State and Delaware.This week you're playing Syracuse. The Orange are only 2-2 and haven't been all that impressive, but you've looked pretty rough yourself. Beau Pribula doesn't seem to be 100%. He's not being used as a runner the same way he was to start the year. He's dropped back to pass 93 times in the last three games, and frankly, Beau Pribula dropping back to pass 31 times per game is not an ideal strategy for him or the Hoos.If you win at home this week, it'll be more of a relief than a sign things have turned back around. But if you lose?
5. TCU Offensive Coordinator Gordon SammisThere's a remarkable stat about TCU this season that I discovered while researching something else entirely this week. Did you know that the Horned Frogs have allowed only 13.4 points per game this season? That's tied for the 12th nationally, and it's tied with Georgia of all teams. Seriously, the Horned Frogs haven't allowed more than 21 points in a game this season.And they're 2-3. The combined record of the 11 teams ahead of them and the Georgia team TCU is tied with? It's 54-3. TCU has as many losses by itself as the other 12 combined. The problem is those other teams are also scoring 41.2 points per game, and TCU is scoring 25.4. That's where Gordon Sammis comes in, because it's not hard to look around the facility and figure out who everybody else is looking at as an easy scapegoat, and Sammis sticks out like a sore thumb.
Sammis was brought in this offseason from UConn after overseeing an offense that scored 35.3 points per game last season and, more importantly, had a QB in Joe Fagnano who threw for 28 touchdowns and only 1 interception. That ball security was a key reason TCU's Sonny Dykes sought out Sammis. After watching Josh Hoover turn the ball over too frequently, Dykes figured he had to pair what looked to be a good defense with an offense that would take care of the ball. They also brought in Harvard transfer Jaden Craig, who was a prolific passer at the Ivy League level.But it hasn't worked. It turns out that it may have been Joe Fagnano who deserved the credit for avoiding turnovers, because TCU ranks 117th nationally with a turnover rate on offense of 14.3%. That's actually slightly worse than last season (113th, 13.2%). To be fair to Jaden Craig, it's not entirely on him. He's thrown four interceptions and fumbled twice, losing one. However, as a team, the Frogs have fumbled the ball 11 times, though they've only lost four of them.In other words, they rank 117th in turnover rate and are actually lucky to rank even that high. It could've been far worse.Now, Sonny Dykes is already on the hot seat and has been included in The Anxiety Rankings earlier this season. He can't fire the QB. He can't fire everybody on the team that's fumbled the ball. But he could fire the new offensive coordinator in a last-ditch effort to save his job. The team is on a bye this week. I hope Sammis spends it wisely.

Welcome to the fifth and final men's basketball power-conference preview for the 2026-27 season here at CBSSports.com. If you'd like to see our predictions for the ACC, Big 12, Big Ten and SEC, just tap those links and enjoy the tour. This is only the start; we've got so much more preview content to come in the three weeks between now and the start of the season.Today we're diving deep into the only basketball-first high-major league in college hoops. I recently wrote about what this year means for the league in a year of transition, including a new commissioner. The Big East could use an injection of some new blood. It would be beneficial for a team or two to overshoot expectations and upset the apple cart, you know?While Rick Pitino's renaissance has been terrific for the Big East's national marketability the past two years — St. John's is the reigning two-time regular-season and tournament champions; no other school has ever done that in the Big East — the league would profit from another team rising up into the Top 25 on a regular basis and threatening the Johnnies and Huskies. Will we see it in 2026-27, or will the Big East again play out as a league with Connecticut and St. John's separating themselves from the rest of the conference? Here's a look at what to know before Villanova tips off the college basketball season on Nov. 1 in Rome against Notre Dame.CBS Sports Big East Preseason Player of the YearSilas Demary Jr. | PG | UConn  Best player on what's expected to be the best team in the conference. A year ago, Demary was tagged as one of the 20 most important transfers in the country. Then he outplayed that high expectation by making our five-man All Transfer Team at season's end for a 34-win Huskies squad that made the national title game. UConn needed an upgrade in physicality, confidence and playmaking at the point; Demary was ready from the jump. He starred in his role, averaging 10.1 points, 5.9 assists, 4.5 rebounds and 1.6 steals. There's a good batch of talent around him again this season, but UConn's chances center on Demary as the head of the snake. He could be just as important and successful for Dan Hurley's program as Tristen Newton was in 2023-24, when Newton modestly guided the Huskies to a second straight national title.
Colben Landrew is making a good first impression for UConn. 
                                                                    Getty Images
                                                            CBS Sports Big East Preseason Freshman of the Year Colben Landrew | SF | UConnSimilar to the past few seasons, the Big East is not expected to be a league that sees an inrush of star power amongst its freshmen. But there will be a name or three to emerge, and our writers believe UConn will have the best of the newbie bunch. Landrew is a 6-6 tweener forward from McComb, Mississippi, who ranked 26th in the class of 2026. He'll come off the bench for Hurley and be a bruiser-type; he also played football in high school before making the full-time switch to hoops. 
Four more players to watch Nigel James Jr. | PG | MarquetteThe league's freshman of the year a season ago, James averaged 16.4 points, 4.9 assists, 3.4 boards and 2.0 steals, emerging as one of the few reasons for optimism in what was a brutal down year at MU. James is said to have a lot of Kam Jones and Tyler Kolek in his approach to the game. If that's the case, he should be able to spearhead a good Marquette roster back into the NCAA Tournament. James' big jump needs to come at the foul line, where he shot 69.2% last season.Tounde Yessoufou | SF | St. John'sThe 6-5 sophomore power wing averaged 17.8 points, 5.9 rebounds, 2.0 steals and 1.6 assists at Baylor. He could be in the NBA right now if he wanted, but returning for one of the best salaries in the Big East with a chance to learn from Pitino and be a star at St. John's was understandably too good to pass up. We expect him to up his game a notch and turn into a top-20 draft pick next June.
Braylon Mullins | SG | UConnMullins (12.0 ppg, 3.5 rpg) also gave some consideration to the draft, but he's got an opportunity to capitalize in multiple ways after cashing one of the most famous shots in NCAA Tournament history. The sophomore wing will be tasked with a lot more this season, and how he handles his increased role after helping author one of the most exhilarating moments in all of American sports in 2026 will be worth monitoring. 
Tyler Perkins | PG | VillanovaThe 6-4 senior guard will need to be Villanova's alpha in order to improve off last season's bounce-back year, which had the Wildcats back wearing home whites in the first round of the NCAA Tournament. Perkins (13.7 ppg, 5.4 rpg) has the ball-handling and pick-and-roll IQ to comfortably keep Nova aloft as a top-five team in the Big East. Can he be the sleeper pick for POY and actually get Nova back to the top of the conference?Big East predicted order of finish
                            
    
                                                
                    
    1. UConnCan UConn get to four Final Fours in a five-year span? It's plausible so long as Dan Hurley is running the show, though we'll note that trusted lieutenants Luke Murray (now the coach at Boston College) and Tom Moore (retirement) are no longer walking the halls in Storrs. Still, UConn is 126-28 the past four seasons with an 18-2 record in the NCAA tourney. So the "can Dan do it again?" storyline will be there so long as UConn's in the mix for a top-three NCAA seed. You read above on Demary and Mullins. Then there's Na'jai Hines, who got off to a nice, if quiet, start as a freshman at Seton Hall. This 5-man might be as impactful defensively as Donovan Clingan was. He's the low-post force that gives the Huskies credence as a preseason top-five team in the country.
Hines and former Duke forward Nik Khamenia are the transfers who will start on Day 1 and be frontcourt anchors. Khamenia left Duke because he was looking for a different role with more offensive opportunities. He's got the potential to be a very nice fit. A familiar name back in the mix is wing Jayden Ross, who has patiently waited for his time. I think it arrives this year with a leadership role attached. Solo Ball is redshirting due to injury, so the Huskies are thinner than desired, but with Landrew coming off the bench and Stanford center Oskar Giltay backing up Hines, this is still — on paper — the safest pick to win the league heading into November.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    2. St. John'sRick Pitino has coached more than 1,500 games in his career across five decades ... and for the first time in his life, he's less than a month out from the start of a season and doesn't know if more than 20% of his roster will be able to play. It's bonkers. But Pitino opted into the courtship of Keyshawn Hall, Reed Bailey, Quinn Ellis and Babacar Sane — four players whose fates await the word from judges in the weeks/months to come — and so here we are. Our guess is it's unlikely all four get eligible, but if they do, then St. John's is borderline top-10 material overall and eye-to-eye with Connecticut.As is, there's still a lot to be excited about in Queens. Right before the withdrawal deadline, former Baylor Bear Tounde Yessoufou committed to St. John's, giving the Red Storm one of the most talented sophomores in the sport. He'll team up with returnees Ian Jackson in the backcourt and 6-11 Ruben Prey as a stretch big. The forecast would be better had Syracuse transfer Donnie Freeman not gone down for the year in the summer with a torn achilles, but the Johnnies still have a ton of hope if Ellis, 23, clears the NCAA's eligibility concerns (over how much money he received prior to enrolling in college). The international takeover in Queens is even more pronounced than at places like Illinois. St. John's has or is trying to roster players whose home countries include Senegal, Sweden, Hungary, Portugal, Serbia, Nigeria and Greece. 

                            
    
                                                
                    
    3. VillanovaAs badly as Villanova fans wanted to see the program continue to sustain itself under Kyle Neptune, last year's immediate turnaround under Kevin Willard (No. 8 seed, 24-9) was proof of why the Neptune era couldn't last longer than three seasons. Now Nova's back into the space where it's projected top-three in the conference, thanks to preseason First-Teamer Tyler Perkins coming back, in addition to Matt Hodge (whose season-ending injury in February torpedoed VU's hopes come March). Gone are Duke Brennan, Bryce Lindsay, Acaden Lewis and Devin Askew, who combined to put up 40-plus points per night, leaving a lot of opportunity for a qualify transfer class led by two preseason all-league notables.The first is PF Kwame Evans Jr. (via Oregon), who could be the guy to connect Villanova's defensive prowess. Another guy with big expectations is Devin Royal (wing, Ohio State), who will start at the 3 and be a veteran glue guy. We think former UIC point guard Elijah Crawford is the one who determines whether Villanova is second/third or fourth/fifth in the league. He can ball out, but how does the jump in league suit him? Two other transfers in the mix, both of whom who averaged 16-plus points last season and might pop as double-digit scorers, are former Cornell guard Jake Fiegen and former St. Bonaventure point Daryl Simmons II. Finally, Italian center Luigi Suigo flirted with the NBA Draft, but he's just beginning to understand how to play at an elevated level, so his outlook is interesting — but no guarantee on production in the first couple of months.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    4. MarquetteMarquette is coming off a god-awful 12-20 campaign that had to be Shaka Smart's worst nightmare, professionally speaking. So, do the Golden Eagles bounce back into the top four of the league this season? That's one of the biggest plot points of the Big East. We, as you can see, expect that to happen. And we think it will happen because MU might have the most valuable player in the conference in sophomore point guard Nigel James Jr. (who you can read more about above). Despite the bad '25-26 go of things, Smart has a loyal culture in Milwaukee. James should shine alongside fellow sophomore Adrien Stevens, who hopes to hit 3s at a 40% clip this season.
The Golden Eagles have nine back from last season, meaning there's more year-over-year consistency here than anywhere else in the Big East (and just about anywhere else in college basketball). Royce Parham (12.5 ppg), Stevens (7.9 ppg) and Damarius Owens (4.8 ppg) are the most notable guys back. But the portal certainly did giveth: Sananada Fru, a stretch 5 who cost a pretty penny, is the key incoming transfer and possibly the guy who can get MU into that top four by season's end. The other transfer is Nolan Minessale, a muscle-bound 3-man from St. Thomas who scored nearly 20/game in the Summit League.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    5. Providence Of the three schools with new coaches, Providence gets the biggest benefit of the doubt in Year 1. Bryan Hodgson quickly proved he had the goods to win immediately at Arkansas State and USF, which is what led him up the East Coast to replace Kim English at PC. Hodgson speaks bluntly, just like his former boss Nate Oats, and wants to represent the PCBC mindset. With eight new guys in the fold, the Friars feel every bit the wild card of the 2026-27 Big East. Dink Pate (who's never played in college but did play for the Westchester Knicks G League franchise) would be a boon to this roster, but sources indicated to CBS Sports in the past week that his eligibility case is unlikely to win out. That in mind, who's going to be the standout Friar over the next five months? We think Miles Byrd is the one. The former San Diego State Aztec arrives via a cross-country flight as a switchable and ultra-durable wing who will be the defensive spirit of this team. He's also likely to jump from 10 points/game to 13 or 14. He'll be set up by Malik Mack, the starting point guard who has familiarity in the league after a couple of years at Georgetown. Those two were welcomed in by Ryan Mela, a Friars holdover from the English era who will start at the wing and probably be good for 10-plus points per game. Six-foot-11 transfer Arrinten Page is expected to start at center. One more name giving PC viability heading into the season is Devin Vanterpool, a lead guard who averaged almost 16 points last season at FAU.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    6. CreightonWhen Alan Huss left High Point after two seasons, an NCAA Tournament appearance and nearly 60 wins, he did so with the promise he would soon take over at Creighton. He waited all of one season, and now that decision has led to one of the best retention situations in the Big East. Jackson McAndrew, Jasen Green, Austin Swartz, Isaac Traudt and Hudson Greer are all back after combining to score about 39 points per night with the Jays. McAndrew dealt with an injury and barely played last season, so there's a good shot that Creighton's first year under Huss will be markedly better than its last one under Greg McDermott, which ended with a 16-18 thud. The transfer who should probably pop is a big that Bluejays fans will have a passing familiarity with. Oswin Erhunmwunse played the past two seasons as a defensive 5-min at Providence. His role will likely lead to a stronger defensive through line with this team. McAndrew, Green and Erhunmwunse pose such a positive threat for Creighton at both ends, it's easy to see the Big East being a six-bid league if our projection turns up true. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    7. XavierThe Musketeers are in their second season under Richard Pitino, but don't bring a lot back from last season's 15-win team that wound up last in the Big East (strange to see Xavier ever finish last). The primary returnee is 6-10 4-man Jovan Milicevic, who ranks among the most underrated players in the conference. Xavier's outlook as an NCAA Tournament team seems to hinge on a five-in-five case: Filip Borovicanin is trying to get another year. He was good for 10.8 points, 7.4 rebounds per game and could step out and shoot. But nobody knows if he'll be cleared. So look for UAB transfer point guard Chance Westry to be a guy who pops in Cincy this season. Westry will be the tallest point in the conference and team up with Miami transfer Tru Washington. Fransfer forward Mike Nwoko cuts a frame that reflects Pitino's clear philosophy from the offseason: he wanted to get tall. Talent-wise, we'll see, but Xavier won't be bullied around.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    8. GeorgetownYear 4 under Ed Cooley brings a serious standards check to D.C. If there's one coach conceivably on the hot seat in this league going into the season, it's Cooley. The Hoyas have averaged 14 wins since he took over, which isn't remotely good enough. Cooley took a chance (and a much bigger paycheck) to leave Providence and alienate himself to that hometown fan base in order to try and resurrect Georgetown. This season feels consequential. The Hoyas bring back forward Caleb Williams (8.8 ppg, 5.1 rpg) and likely reserve guard Kayvaun Mulready, but otherwise there's a lot of wait-and-see. The biggest question is Vince Iwuchukwu's eligibility. The center is trying to get a fifth year, but his chances are foggy. 
Inbound talents include: Chol Machot (Charleston), Elmarko Jackson (Kansas) and Jaland Lowe (Kentucky), all three of whom will guarantee Georgetown is better than eighth in the conference if they max out their potential. Vyctorius Miller (Oklahoma State) is the other piece, and a likely starter, who will be a factor. If Iwuchukwu winds up playing and this team stays healthy, you can squint and see an outcome that has Georgetown in the top five at the end-of-year standings. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    9. DePaulThe Blue Demons have made genuine strides in two years under Chris Holtmann, going from 304th at KenPom at the end of the Tony Stubblefield era to 122nd in Holtmann's first year and 99th in 2025-26. Look for DePaul to nudge up again nationally, even if we've collectively slotted them ninth. The most valuable player is probably senior guard Layden Blocker (11.1 points and 3.5 assists last season), but Magoon Gwath's move from SDSU to Chicago could be one of the most consequential transfers in the Big East. Gwath battled injuries last season, but was the Mountain West's best defender in 2024-25. He might be a top-two defensive big in this conference over the next five months. Toss in Tulsa transfer Ade Popoola (41.2 3-pt%) and UTRGV wing Koree Cotton (40.3%) and the Demons should have some solid balance. Holtmann scheduled up a bit, which should give us real indicators by December if this team can contend for the NCAAs.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    10. Seton HallShaheen Holloway had the lowest budget of any Big East school this offseason, so the challenge is steep yet again. The Hall brings in 13 new faces, including nine portal pickups, after finishing 21-12. Keep in mind, SHU was the preseason pick in October 2025 to be the conference's worst team; Holloway wound up winning Big East Coach of the Year. Sophomore guard Trey Parker is the only carryover from last season. Roddie Anderson III, who put up 11 points per game at Xavier, should see the floor a ton, as will Simeon Wilcher. The former high-end prospect has bounced from St. John's to Texas to SHU. Is this the year he pops? Another guy we're intrigued about is Terry Copeland Jr., who is a 6-9, 270-pound big who ranked as the best JUCO player in the country last season. If he translates to D-I, it'll be huge for Seton Hall's physical viability, which is of course Holloway's calling card. 

                            
    
                                                
                    
    11. ButlerThe last of the three schools with new coaches in the league. BU alum Ronald Nored is now in charge after a decade working in the NBA and G League. The 36-year-old was the point guard for those Bulldog teams that made back-to-back national title games in 2010 and '11. Now Nored is tasked with lifting Butler back into the rotation of being a top-six program in the conference, an assignment that may take a few years to materialize. Nored was able to keep point guard Jalen Jackson and center Drayton Jones, which is a nice starting point, but this is a big build mostly from scratch. Two inbound transfers who will be asked to contribute in a big way are Jordan Ellerbee (13.1 ppg at FGCU) and Treyson Anderson (10.4 ppg at North Dakota State). Butler is the popular pick to finish in the Big East basement, but typically the team forecasted last in October doesn't wind up as the No. 11 seed when the Big East Tournament is played in March.Big East expert picks

title: Sydney Colson slams ex-Fever teammate Sophie Cunningham for outspoken opinions - CBS Sports
description: Cunningham's stance on transgender athletes struck a nerve with her former teammate
body:
Cunningham's stance on transgender athletes struck a nerve with her former teammate
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 9, 2026
                            
                    at
    12:36 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Sydney Colson this week blasted Sophie Cunningham, her former Indiana Fever teammate, for controversial remarks Cunningham made earlier this year to ESPN centered around her stance against transgender women participating in women's sports. Colson, a two-time WNBA champion who played in 30 games in 2025 for the Fever, discussed Cunningham's opinions on her podcast. "For the white players in the league, when you don't say s---, and even worse, when you say things that are harmful, talking about the trans s---, nobody respects you," she said. "Shut the f--- up, shut the f--- up. Nobody wants to hear your opinion. Freedom of speech, so you can say it, but just know -- people are just trying to get by when they're dealing with you. "You ought to be ashamed, y'all ought to be ashamed to act like you're cool with people, to act like you care about sisterhood, all of these things."
Cunningham previously said this season she wanted to "protect young girls in the locker room" and added "they shouldn't have to go against biological men."She doesn't view herself as an activist, but did not backtrack on her statements."I said what I said. I think it's kind of common sense," Cunningham said. "And I think I'll always believe in that. I think it's really important to protect children, and that's little girls who are also involved in that category. I stand on what I said."

        
            
                Caitlin Clark denounces fan rhetoric, addresses next contract and backs Fever coach in exit interview
                
                    Jack Maloney                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
In August, the WNBA players' association released a statement declaring its belief in diversity and inclusion, saying it will "not be used as political pawns" in response to the league being thrust into the center of political debate. "The WNBPA represents 200+ individual people with different lived experiences, cultures, lifestyles and opinions," the statement read. "We embrace justice, equity, diversity, and inclusion. Those are the values that unite this Union and allow it to protect women's sports while creating transformational change. Hate, abuse, and demonization of any person or group of people, including transgender people, only fuel fear, division, and harm. We will continue to have hard conversations. But we will not be used as political pawns."Cunningham is currently an unrestricted free agent after her one-year, $665,000 contract with the Fever expired after the team's first-round playoff loss to the Las Vegas Aces. She spent the last two seasons with the Fever after six seasons with the Phoenix Mercury to begin her career. 
After Indiana's playoff elimination, Cunningham showed up to last week's Florida vs. Missouri football game donning a hat with "No Cis, Just... Woman" scripted on it."I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans and I'm like, 'I never once said that.' I think that I am here to extend love," Cunningham told ESPN previously.Colson said she lost respect for her former teammate."Listen, if you never speak up about a damn thing when you know it's impacting the people you claim to love, care about, you know, fighting together as a team, sisters and you don't speak up when things affect them ... they don't respect you, they're just trying to make it," Colson said.

title: Tributes pour in as NFL world mourns, remembers football giant and HOFer Mike Ditka - CBS Sports
description: A Hall of Fame coach who guided the iconic 1985 Bears to a Super Bowl XX title, Ditka won 106 games in Chicago, s
body:
A Hall of Fame coach who guided the iconic 1985 Bears to a Super Bowl XX title, Ditka won 106 games in Chicago, second in franchise history
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 9, 2026
                            
                    at
    12:51 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Legendary head coach Mike Ditka died at the age of 86 on Friday. A football giant, Ditka is a member of both the College Football Hall of Fame and Pro Football Hall of Fame. The former tight end won Offensive Rookie of the Year in 1961 with the Chicago Bears after racking up 1,076 receiving yards and 12 touchdowns in his first NFL season — the perfect way to start a 12-year career that saw him win Super Bowl VI with the Dallas Cowboys.Ditka retired following the 1972 season and began his coaching career as an assistant under Tom Landry in Dallas. The Cowboys made three Super Bowls during his tenure, winning one (XII). In 1982, the Bears, who drafted Ditka No. 5 overall out of Pittsburgh, hired him to be their new head coach. Chicago made the NFC Championship game in 1984, and then went 15-1 in 1985 on the way to a Super Bowl XX win over the New England Patriots. It remains the Bears' lone Super Bowl title. 
Ditka registered seven double-digit win seasons in his 11 years with the Bears, won NFL Coach of the Year in 1985 and 1988, and made seven playoff appearances with three NFC Championship appearances. His 106 wins rank second in franchise history behind George Halas, who coached Chicago for four decades. No Bears head coach has held their post for more than nine years other than Ditka and Halas. He wrapped up his coaching career with the New Orleans Saints, going 15-33 over three seasons. "Mike Ditka epitomized football over so many years," NFL commissioner Roger Goodell said in a statement. "He brought intensity, authenticity, and an unmistakable personality to everything he did. As a Hall of Fame player, Super Bowl-winning coach with his beloved and iconic Bears, and as a broadcaster, Mike served as an ambassador for the game and inspired generations of fans. Through his work with the Gridiron Greats Assistance Fund, Mike was a champion for taking care of those who helped build our game. We extend our deepest condolences to Diana and the Ditka family."
Ditka is one of two men to win a Super Bowl as a player, assistant coach and head coach in NFL history, joining fellow Hall of Famer Tom Flores. Reactions around the football world poured in to mourn the loss of a legendary leader. That includes Walter Payton's son, Jarrett, who shared a statement from the Ditka family. "It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and friend, Mike Ditka. While the world knew Mike as a Hall of Fame football player, legendary coach, and leader of the Chicago Bears' Super Bowl XX championship team, we knew him as the heart of our family. Mike will be missed beyond measure and remembered forever. With love and gratitude, The Ditka Family."
